idiom_name: static func + (lhs:rhs:) on an immutable struct (optionally conforming to AdditiveArithmetic)
implementation_notes: Swift declares closure as an operator method on the type: static func + (lhs: Money, rhs: Money) -> Money in a struct with let properties, so a + b yields Money and value semantics (structs copy on assignment) prevent the operands from aliasing. What replaces the classic structure is that operator method plus struct immutability - the standard library's own types are the model - and, when generic accumulation is wanted, conformance to AdditiveArithmetic, which supplies the zero element and the +,- family so reduce(.zero, +) works over your type. Keep the named method form for combinations that are not additive (intersection, merge), and remember that operations returning a new value on every call are the default, so hot paths should use the value-type optimisations rather than in-place mutation.
pitfalls: Integer overflow traps at runtime in Swift: a closed-looking + crashes instead of returning a wrong value, so use addingReportingOverflow or validate the range if amounts can reach the limit.

AdditiveArithmetic requires a single static zero, but a Money that carries its currency has no standalone neutral element - model zero(for:) and skip the conformance unless the identity is genuinely total.
Operator methods must be static on the type; an instance method named + never participates in operator dispatch, and globally declared custom operators can collide with or obscure the standard ones.
Using a class instead of a struct reintroduces reference aliasing, so the pattern's guarantee disappears unless the class is genuinely immutable.
